strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem with a coherent design: quantizing the combined pretrained weights and LoRA updates enables low-bit inference without a separate adapter path, while allowing quantization parameters to adapt during fine-tuning.

The evaluation covers several model families and sizes, 3-bit and 4-bit quantization, seven commonsense tasks, and zero-shot/five-shot MMLU. Some improvements are substantial: on LLaMA-2 7B at 3 bits, L4Q achieves 61.3 commonsense accuracy versus 57.6 for QLoRA* and 56.3 for QA-LoRA.

The paper reports practical resource measurements and useful initialization, rank, and group-size ablations. The reported 7B training memory of 25.4 GB, compared with 25.1 GB for LoRA and 79.5 GB for QAT, supports a meaningful efficiency contribution. Inference comparisons use the same quantized kernel and examine multiple batch sizes.
weaknesses: Reproducibility remains insufficiently specified for a clear Findings recommendation. The manuscript links upstream libraries but provides no L4Q implementation link or detailed account of tensors saved versus recomputed in its custom backward pass. LoRA scaling, target modules, microbatch size, and activation checkpointing are also unspecified. Figure 3 describes 100 training steps, whereas Appendix B describes 12,800 iterations with batch size 128; optimizer updates and accumulation microsteps need to be distinguished explicitly.

The backward equations require clarification. In Equations 29–30, the clipping condition has the shape of the full weight matrix, whereas the resulting gradients have adapter shapes. With G = (dL/dY)X^T and an elementwise clipping mask M, the gradients should be alpha B^T(G ⊙ M) and alpha(G ⊙ M)A^T. The mask must be applied before matrix contraction. This may be a notation problem, but the current presentation does not establish whether the implementation handles it correctly.

The largest-model efficiency comparison is confounded: Appendix D uses sequence length 128 for L4Q on 33B, versus 2048 for the other settings. Its memory and training-time results therefore do not establish efficiency under matched workloads. L4Q also receives half as many training iterations as PTQ-based methods; the single training-loss curve provides limited evidence for general claims about faster convergence. Matched-context measurements and validation quality versus training compute would strengthen these claims.

The baseline results establish performance against modified uniform-quantization versions of QLoRA and LoftQ. They do not establish superiority over those methods in their original configurations. LoftQ* frequently falls near chance on 3-bit MMLU, yet its learning rates and configuration validation are not reported. A fine-tune–merge–PTQ baseline would also directly test whether joint optimization improves quality over a simple alternative producing the same inference format.

The accuracy conclusions exceed the demonstrated consistency and precision. Several gains are only 0.1–0.3 percentage points, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, and exceptions exist: LLaMA-2 13B at 3 bits scores 50.0 on five-shot MMLU versus 50.6 for QLoRA*. Evaluation uses one instruction-tuning corpus and multiple-choice benchmarks, limiting evidence about instruction-following quality. These limitations warrant narrower claims and targeted validation.
